\section[lo siento]{lo siento — \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C20-lo-siento}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know \textbf{por favor}, \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} — the fourth courtesy word is \textbf{lo siento}, \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry.\textquotedblright{} Spanish doesn't say \textquotedblleft{}I am sorry\textquotedblright{} as an adjective; it says something closer to \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I feel this.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lo} = \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} — a neuter pronoun pointing at the situation itself, not a specific noun.
  \item \textbf{siento} = \textquotedblleft{}I feel,\textquotedblright{} from the verb \textbf{sentir}, \textquotedblleft{}to feel,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{sentīre}. That root gave English a whole family: \textbf{sentiment}, \textbf{sense}, \textbf{consent} (\textquotedblleft{}feel together\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{resent} (\textquotedblleft{}feel again/against\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{lo siento} is literally \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}} — you're naming the feeling (regret, sympathy) rather than declaring a state. It's the Spanish you reach for both to apologize (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{lo siento}, I stepped on your foot\textquotedblright{}) and to console (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{lo siento mucho},\textquotedblright{} I'm so sorry, on hearing sad news).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish keeps a \textbf{second} word for a different job. \textbf{Perdón} (\textquotedblleft{}pardon\textquotedblright{}), from \textbf{perdonar} — Latin \textbf{per-} (\textquotedblleft{}thoroughly\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{dōnāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to give,\textquotedblright{} the same root as English \textbf{donate} and \textbf{condone}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to give completely},\textquotedblright{} i.e. to forgive. \textbf{Perdón} is what you say to:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item get someone's \textbf{attention} or squeeze past them (like English \textquotedblleft{}excuse me\textquotedblright{}),
  \item ask forgiveness for something \textbf{you did wrong} (a real apology, often stronger than \emph{lo siento}).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Lo siento} leans toward \textbf{regret/sympathy} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry that happened\textquotedblright{}), while \textbf{perdón} leans toward \textbf{fault and forgiveness} (\textquotedblleft{}excuse me / forgive me\textquotedblright{}). Native speakers reach for whichever fits — the boundary is soft, and mixing them up is not a real mistake, just a shade off.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}siento\textquotedblright{} — I feel — then \textquotedblleft{}lo siento,\textquotedblright{} I feel it / I'm sorry{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the cousin word — \textquotedblleft{}perdón,\textquotedblright{} pardon / excuse me{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: both together in your head: regret vs. forgiveness{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{lo siento} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{siento} \textquotedblleft{}I feel,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{sentīre}, like English \emph{sentiment}.) What's the other Spanish word for sorry/excuse-me, and how is it different? (\textbf{Perdón}, \textquotedblleft{}pardon\textquotedblright{} — leans toward fault and forgiveness, or getting someone's attention, while \emph{lo siento} leans toward regret and sympathy.)
\end{tcolorbox}
